link.title: Training a Model You Plan to Serve

entry.content:
Inference from First Principles 1. What a token costs 2. Fitting a model onto a rack 3. Reading the price sheet 4. Training a model you plan to serve

Part 4 of 4

Once a model will serve hundreds of trillions of tokens, the cheapest plan is to train a smaller model for far longer than Chinchilla suggests. A rough estimate of how much longer.

Inference from First Principles · 4 diagrams

From Parts 1 to 3

Serving cost per token is set by compute when batches are large and by memory traffic when they're small or contexts are long. Prefill runs near the compute floor, decode is memory-bound, and a frontier provider serves on the order of a billion tokens per second across its models. Compute costs scale with the number of active parameters, \(N_{\text{active}}\). Memory costs scale with total parameters and KV cache size.

Parts 1 to 3 were about serving a model that already exists. This part steps back to the decision before that: how big should the model be, and how much data should it be trained on? The Chinchilla paper answered that for the case where only training compute counts, and the answer works out to about 20 training tokens per parameter. A model that will go on to serve hundreds of trillions of tokens should be smaller than that and trained for much longer.

  • A model's lifetime compute splits into pre-training, reinforcement learning (RL), and serving. A smaller model trained for longer costs more to train and less to serve.
  • When one cost falls and another rises, the total is usually close to its minimum where the two are roughly equal. Here that means spending similar amounts on pre-training, RL, and serving.
  • In tokens, that works out to about as many serving tokens as pre-training tokens, and somewhat fewer RL tokens, because RL runs at lower hardware efficiency.
  • At today's serving volumes, that points to frontier models being pre-trained on hundreds of trillions of tokens, a hundred to a few hundred times Chinchilla-optimal. Open models are already trained 20 to nearly 100 times past it.

Where a model's compute goes

Over its life, a model consumes compute in three phases.

Pre-training costs \(6N_{\text{active}}D_{\text{pre}}\) FLOPs: 2 per parameter per token for the forward pass and 4 for the backward pass. RL first generates rollouts, which is decode at 2 FLOPs per parameter per token, and then trains on some of them, which adds 4 more for those tokens, so it costs between \(2N\) and \(6N\) per RL token. Serving costs \(2N_{\text{active}}\) per token.

FLOPs aren't the whole cost, though. What you pay for is GPU time, which is FLOPs divided by the throughput you actually achieve. Pre-training is compute-bound and can keep a large fraction of the hardware busy. RL generation and serving are dominated by decode, which, as Parts 1 and 3 showed, spends most of its time waiting on memory. So write each cost as FLOPs over a utilization factor \(u\):

\[ C_{\text{pre}} \propto \frac{6\,N D_{\text{pre}}}{u_{\text{pre}}}, \qquad C_{\text{RL}} \propto \frac{m\,N D_{\text{RL}}}{u_{\text{RL}}}, \qquad C_{\text{inf}} \propto \frac{2\,N D_{\text{inf}}}{u_{\text{inf}}} \]

with \(m\) between 2 and 6.

A rule of thumb for balancing costs

Making the model smaller lowers the serving cost and the per-token cost of training. But a smaller model needs more training tokens to reach the same quality, and past the Chinchilla point that trade gets worse quickly. So for a fixed quality target, one cost falls with model size and the other rises. Where is the total lowest?

There's a general heuristic here. If you're minimizing \(F(x) + G(x)\) where \(F\) falls and \(G\) rises, the minimum is often near the point where \(F = G\). For power laws it's easy to make exact. With \(F = a\,x^{-p}\) and \(G = b\,x^{q}\), setting the derivative of the sum to zero gives

\[ p\,F = q\,G \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{F}{G} = \frac{q}{p} \]

at the minimum. If the exponents are similar, the two costs are equal there. If one exponent is twice the other, the costs differ by a factor of two. And near the minimum the total curve is flat, so landing a bit off costs little. Scaling laws are roughly power laws, so the heuristic should hold to within a small factor near the Chinchilla point. Far from it, the training curve steepens, which makes \(p\) larger and means training should cost somewhat less than serving at the optimum. Checking this properly would mean fitting real scaling-law exponents, which labs don't publish.

Setting the three costs equal

Apply the heuristic to all three phases and set \(C_{\text{pre}} \approx C_{\text{RL}} \approx C_{\text{inf}}\). Treating RL as a third equal share is a further simplification, since how much RL to do is its own choice. The active parameter count \(N\) appears in every term, so it cancels:

\[ \frac{6\,D_{\text{pre}}}{u_{\text{pre}}} \approx \frac{m\,D_{\text{RL}}}{u_{\text{RL}}} \approx \frac{2\,D_{\text{inf}}}{u_{\text{inf}}} \]

Writing the costs this way folds every memory cost into the utilization factors. That hides the fact that KV reads and weight reads don't scale with \(N_{\text{active}}\), so treat what follows as an order of magnitude.

Now we need the utilizations. Pre-training is the most efficient of the three. Serving mixes efficient prefill with memory-bound decode, and RL generation is mostly decode. As a rough assumption, say both RL and serving get about a third of pre-training's utilization. Then

\[ D_{\text{inf}} = 3\,\frac{u_{\text{inf}}}{u_{\text{pre}}}\,D_{\text{pre}} \approx D_{\text{pre}}, \qquad D_{\text{RL}} = \frac{6}{m}\,\frac{u_{\text{RL}}}{u_{\text{pre}}}\,D_{\text{pre}} \approx \tfrac{2}{3}\,D_{\text{pre}} \ \ (\text{for } m = 3) \]

To within the factors we can't pin down, a model should serve about as many tokens as it was pre-trained on, and do somewhat fewer RL tokens than either. If you split the cost 50/50 between training and serving instead of three ways, the answer moves by less than a factor of two.

There's one adjustment that pushes the other way. A lab doesn't know in advance how popular a model will be or how long it will last before something better replaces it. Some models get replaced quickly, and some never catch on. So the expected number of serving tokens is less than the hoped-for number, and a cautious lab should plan for somewhat less over-training than this simple balance suggests.

Plugging in numbers

Serving volume is the one number in this calculation that providers publish, at least in aggregate. Google said in May 2026 that it was processing more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month across its products, about 1.2 billion tokens per second. That's spread across many models and surfaces. Say one flagship model handles 100 million tokens per second, and it stays the flagship for three months, about 7.9 million seconds:

\[ D_{\text{inf}} \approx 10^{8}\ \text{tokens/s} \times 7.9 \times 10^{6}\ \text{s} \approx 8 \times 10^{14}\ \text{tokens} \]

That's about 800 trillion tokens. Two things push it down. Google's count includes input tokens, many of them cache hits that cost far less than a fresh forward pass, and the popularity discount from the previous section applies. Call it a few hundred trillion tokens of serving, which by the balance argument means a few hundred trillion tokens of pre-training.

Compare that with Chinchilla. Frontier labs don't publish active parameter counts, but something around 100 billion is plausible. At 20 tokens per parameter, Chinchilla-optimal training would be about 2 trillion tokens. A few hundred trillion is a hundred to a few hundred times that.

That sounds extreme until you look at open models, where the numbers are published:

DeepSeek-V3 was trained about 20 times past Chinchilla-optimal and Kimi K2 about 24 times. Qwen3-235B-A22B went about 82 times past it, and Llama 3 8B about 94 times. The small models' high ratios come partly from labs reusing one dataset across a model family. Llama 3 70B and 405B saw about the same 15 trillion tokens as the 8B, which is about 11 and 2 times Chinchilla-optimal for them. So these numbers show that heavy over-training is normal practice, but they aren't a clean test of the serving argument. The frontier estimate rests on the calculation above.

There are two caveats. Chinchilla's 20 tokens per parameter was fit on dense models, and active parameters are only a rough stand-in for an MoE model's size. And there may not be a few hundred trillion tokens of good text in the world. Reaching numbers like that means repeating data, generating synthetic data, or training on other modalities. The balance argument tells you where the optimum is, not whether you can get there.

The argument also says something about the scale of serving. Pre-training data is a large share of all the text people have written down, plus whatever else labs can find or make. For the training to be well spent, the model should write back about as much as it read.

The whole model on one page

Every result in this series came from a handful of formulas and constants. Here they are in one place, with a note on how solid each number is.

Quantity Formula or value Basis
Compute time per step \(2BN_{\text{active}}/\text{FLOPS}\) Definition
Memory time per step \((\beta N_{\text{total}} + B\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}})/\text{BW}\) Definition
Hardware ratio \(R\) \(\dfrac{\text{FLOPS}/2}{\text{BW}/\beta} \approx 300\) Spec sheets: H100 about 295, GB200 about 310
Balance batch \(B^{*} \approx R \times N_{\text{total}}/N_{\text{active}}\) Derived. DeepSeek-V3 about 5,400
Step time with full HBM HBM capacity / bandwidth, 20 to 40 ms Spec sheets
Latency floor \(\beta N_{\text{total}}/(E \times \text{BW}_{\text{per GPU}})\) Derived
Scale-up vs. scale-out bandwidth About 10× (9 to 18×) Spec sheets
Rack boundary is cheap when \(2kL \gtrsim 10\) Derived
Memory per GPU with pipelining \(\beta N_{\text{total}}/(EP) + b\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}/E\) Derived
KV size from a price step \(s_{\text{kv}} \approx \beta N_{\text{active}}/(R\,n_{\text{ctx}})\) Assumes the step sits at the crossover and \(N_{\text{active}}\) is guessed
Best storage tier for hold time \(T\) \(T \approx\) capacity / bandwidth Heuristic
Lifetime compute split \(6D_{\text{pre}}/u_{\text{pre}} \approx mD_{\text{RL}}/u_{\text{RL}} \approx 2D_{\text{inf}}/u_{\text{inf}}\) Heuristic. Utilizations assumed

None of these numbers is precise, and several are guesses. But they hang together. The same two hardware ratios explain why batches hold thousands of sequences, why a step takes tens of milliseconds, why fast modes cost what they do, why output tokens and long contexts cost more, why cache hits are cheap, and why models are trained on so much more data than Chinchilla recommends. When a new chip, model, or price sheet comes out, you can usually place it with the same few divisions.

Diagrams are drawn in TikZ.

entry.title: Reading the API Price Sheet
entry.content:
Inference from First Principles 1. What a token costs 2. Fitting a model onto a rack 3. Reading the price sheet 4. Training a model you plan to serve

Part 3 of 4

Long-context surcharges, output tokens that cost more than input tokens, and cheap cache hits all fall out of the same cost model. Here is what each one tells us.

Inference from First Principles · 6 diagrams

From Parts 1 and 2

A decode step takes at least \(\max(t_{\text{compute}}, t_{\text{memory}})\), with \(t_{\text{compute}} \approx 2BN_{\text{active}}/\text{FLOPS}\) and \(t_{\text{memory}} \approx (\beta N_{\text{total}} + B\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}})/\text{BW}\). A GPU does about \(R \approx 300\) multiply-adds in the time it takes to read one weight. At scale, decode spends most of its time reading KV cache. A model is served from one scale-up domain, usually a rack.

AI labs don't publish their architectures, but they do publish prices. Prices can't stay far above cost for long, because a competitor would undercut them, and they can't stay below cost for long either. So the shape of a price sheet carries information about the hardware and the model behind it. This part reads the common features of LLM price sheets with the cost model from Parts 1 and 2.

  • A long-context surcharge may mark the point where reading the KV cache starts to cost more than the compute. Treating one price step as that crossover suggests a KV cache of only a few kilobytes per token, which takes aggressive compression.
  • Output tokens cost 4 to 8 times as much as input tokens because prefill shares its memory traffic across many tokens per pass, while decode reads everything for a single token per sequence. A 5x price ratio suggests decode spends about five times as long on memory as on compute.
  • Cache hits cost a tenth of a normal input token or less because storing the KV cache and copying it back is much cheaper than recomputing it. The relative prices of short and long cache durations point at flash storage, not HBM.
  • Very long contexts stay expensive because the memory traffic of decode grows linearly with context, and memory bandwidth improves only a little each hardware generation.

The cost of a longer context

Take one sequence in a big batch and ask what each new output token costs as its context grows. The compute per token barely changes: the model multiplies by the same active weights whether the context is short or long. The memory traffic per token grows, because each step reads the KV cache for every earlier token. With the batch large enough to amortize the weights, the memory time per token is about \(n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}/\text{BW}\), a straight line in the context length.

Below the crossover, a longer context is almost free, because the chip is waiting on compute anyway. Above it, every extra token of context adds cost. A provider that charges one flat rate either overcharges short prompts or loses money on long ones, so some use two tiers. When Google launched Gemini 3 Pro, it charged $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens for prompts up to 200K tokens, and $4 and $18 for longer prompts, with the whole request billed at the higher rate.

Not every provider does this. Anthropic prices the full million-token window of its recent large models at one flat rate, while its small Haiku 5.5 model charges five times as much once a prompt passes 100,000 tokens. Both fit the cost model. A small model does little compute per token, so KV reads overtake compute at a shorter context. A flat price on a large model suggests a very small KV cache per token, or long requests being averaged in with short ones.

Reading the KV cache size off a price step

Suppose the 200K-token step sits near the crossover. That's an assumption, but it's the natural place to put a price step. At the crossover, the KV read time per token equals the compute time per token:

\[ \frac{n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}}{\text{BW}} = \frac{2\,N_{\text{active}}}{\text{FLOPS}} \]

Solve for the KV cache size per token, and use the hardware ratio \(R = (\text{FLOPS}/2)/(\text{BW}/\beta) \approx 300\) from Part 1:

\[ s_{\text{kv}} = \frac{\beta\,N_{\text{active}}}{R\;n_{\text{ctx}}} \]

We don't know the active parameter count of a frontier model. A hundred billion is a reasonable guess. With 8-bit weights (\(\beta = 1\)) and \(n_{\text{ctx}} = 200{,}000\),

\[ s_{\text{kv}} \approx \frac{10^{11}}{300 \times 2 \times 10^{5}} \approx 1{,}700\ \text{bytes per token} \]

If the model had 50 billion active parameters, it would be about 830 bytes. At 200 billion, about 3.3 KB. Either way it comes out at a few kilobytes at most. Is that plausible? The KV cache per token is

\[ s_{\text{kv}} = (\text{layers with their own KV}) \times 2 \times (\text{KV heads}) \times d_{\text{head}} \times (\text{bytes per value}) \]

where the 2 counts keys and values. Plug in a few real and hypothetical designs:

A plain grouped-query attention model like Llama 3 70B stores about 328 KB per token. DeepSeek-V3 compresses keys and values into one small latent vector per layer and gets down to about 70 KB. Reaching a couple of kilobytes takes tricks that stack:

  • Share one KV cache across many layers. Character.AI described sharing KV caches between neighboring layers, combined with a single KV head and mostly local attention, and reported that together these cut KV cache size by more than 20 times.
  • Make most layers local. Gemma 3 uses five sliding-window layers, which only look back 1,024 tokens, for every global layer. Only the global layers' caches grow with context.
  • Compress keys and values, as DeepSeek's latent attention does.
  • Read only part of the cache. Sparse attention schemes such as DeepSeek's DSA pick a subset of past tokens for each new token. The full cache is still stored, but each step reads less of it, which lowers the bandwidth cost per token even though the capacity cost stays.

A combination of these can plausibly reach a few kilobytes per token of long-range context. The estimate has big error bars. The price step may not sit exactly at the crossover, prices include margins, and the active parameter count is a guess. But it points at kilobytes, not hundreds of kilobytes, and the gap matters. At 70 KB per token, a million-token context is 70 GB per sequence, more than a third of a GB200 GPU's HBM. At 2 KB it's 2 GB.

Why output tokens cost more than input tokens

Most price sheets charge 4 to 8 times as much for output tokens as for input tokens. Anthropic charges 5 times as much, Gemini 3 Pro 6 times, and GPT-5 8 times. The reason is the difference between prefill and decode.

Text the model didn't write, such as the system prompt, the user's message, a file, or a tool result, is known all at once. So the model can push all of those tokens through in a single pass. That's prefill. Text the model writes has to come out one token per pass. That's decode.

Now look at the cost of one pass that handles \(n\) new tokens per sequence. The memory traffic is the same as for a decode step: read the weights once, and read each sequence's existing KV cache once. The new tokens' keys and values are computed on the chip as part of the pass. The compute is \(n\) times larger, so the cost per token is

\[ \frac{t}{n} \approx \max\!\left(\frac{2\,N_{\text{active}}}{\text{FLOPS}},\ \ \frac{\beta N_{\text{total}}/B + n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}}{n \cdot \text{BW}}\right) \]

per sequence in the batch. The memory term is divided by \(n\).

Prefill passes cover hundreds or thousands of tokens, so the memory term disappears and prefill runs at the compute floor. Decode is the \(n = 1\) case, where the memory term is as large as it gets. If prices track costs, an output price five times the input price says that in decode, the memory time per token is roughly five times the compute time. Part 1's DeepSeek-V3 example, with HBM full of 30,000-token contexts at 70 KB per token, had KV reads at about 17 times compute. The gap means that either typical serving is less KV-heavy than that example, through shorter contexts or smaller KV caches per token, or output prices don't track decode cost closely. A KV cache of a few kilobytes per token, as the previous section suggested, would close most of it, because many more sequences would fit in HBM and the compute per step would rise to match.

Prefill isn't free of its own long-context cost, though. Each prompt token attends to every token before it, and in prefill that attention costs real compute as well as memory traffic. In Llama 3 70B, attention's multiply-adds per token equal the weight multiply-adds at about 53,000 tokens of context (80 layers times 64 query heads of width 128, for both the key and value products, against 70 billion weights). Long prompts get expensive to prefill too, which is another reason input prices step up for very long prompts.

Why cache hits are cheap

Prompt caching lets you reuse the KV cache for a prefix you've sent before, such as a long system prompt or a codebase. Anthropic's prices for its Claude 4.x models, as multiples of the normal input price, are:

Operation Price vs. normal input
Normal input (no caching) 1×
Write to cache, kept 5 minutes 1.25×
Write to cache, kept 1 hour 2×
Read from cache (a hit) 0.1×

Its newest models charge even less for a hit: 0.05× for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, and 0.025× for the Fable models. The write prices are the same.

There are two ways to get a prefix's KV cache onto the GPUs. You can compute it from the token IDs, which means running prefill again. Or you can have kept it somewhere and copy it back. A cache miss means you threw it away and have to recompute it. The gap of 10 times or more between a normal input token and a cache hit is the gap between those two options.

Where do you keep it? Each storage tier has two costs for holding data. Holding it takes capacity, for as long as you hold it. Getting it back takes bandwidth, once. Recomputing has no holding cost but a large retrieval cost. HBM has a large holding cost, since HBM is the most expensive memory in the system, but costs nothing to retrieve from, because the data is already where it's needed. Host DRAM and flash are much cheaper to hold data in, but the data has to be copied back into HBM before use.

A storage device is used efficiently when its capacity and its bandwidth run out at about the same time. If you're holding data for time \(T\) and then reading it once, that happens when

\[ T \approx \frac{\text{capacity}}{\text{bandwidth}} \]

which is the device's drain time, the time to read the whole thing once. It's the same balance argument as compute against memory in Part 1, applied to capacity against bandwidth. Database designers know a version of it as the five-minute rule, from Jim Gray and Franco Putzolu's 1987 paper on when to keep data in memory versus on disk.

Both cache durations land in flash territory. HBM is far too expensive for this. Its drain time is about 25 ms, so holding a prompt there for five minutes costs about 12,000 times as much as reading it once. Host DRAM fits hold times of seconds. Flash fits minutes to a couple of hours, which covers both. Hard disks would suit data held for a day.

The prices fit this picture in one more way. A cache write has to run prefill anyway, which costs the normal 1×. So the extra 0.25× for a five-minute write is the price of holding the data for five minutes, and the extra 1× for a one-hour write is the price of holding it for an hour.

Holding for 12 times as long costs only 4 times as much. If both durations used the same storage at the same rate, the hour would cost 3× extra, not 1×. That's consistent with the hour living on cheaper storage, such as larger, slower flash drives, whose drain times run to hours. Prices aren't costs, and a provider may simply round to friendly numbers, so treat this as a hint.

Why long contexts stay expensive

Context windows went from 2,048 tokens in GPT-3 (2020) to 8K and 32K in GPT-4 (early 2023), then to 128K and 200K by the end of 2023, and to a million with Gemini 1.5 in early 2024, later two million. Llama 4 Scout claims ten million. Several flagship models offer a million tokens today. Advertised windows keep growing, but serving very long contexts at scale stays expensive, and the cost model says why.

The compute per token barely depends on context length. The memory traffic per decoded token grows in proportion to it, and so does the memory each sequence occupies. Fewer long sequences fit in HBM at once, so batches shrink and the weights are amortized over fewer tokens. HBM bandwidth improves by a factor of two or so per hardware generation, which doesn't come close to keeping up with 10x or 100x jumps in context.

One argument against needing continual learning is that a model could learn on the job in context, if it could hold, say, a month of work. That might be a hundred million tokens. At 70 KB per token that's 7 TB per sequence, more than half of an NVL72's entire HBM. Even at 2 KB per token, it's 200 GB per sequence. Sparse attention reduces how much each step reads, but it still has to store everything, and attending to too few past tokens hurts quality. Contexts that long will need architectural changes as well as faster memory.

In Part 4, the last part, we turn from serving to training and ask how much data a model should be trained on, given how many tokens it will serve.

entry.title: Fitting a Model onto a Rack

link.title: Fitting a Model onto a Rack

entry.content:
Inference from First Principles 1. What a token costs 2. Fitting a model onto a rack 3. Reading the price sheet 4. Training a model you plan to serve

Part 2 of 4

How mixture-of-experts models are spread across GPUs, why one rack is the natural unit, and what pipelining across racks does and does not buy you.

Inference from First Principles · 8 diagrams

From Part 1

A decode step takes at least \(\max(t_{\text{compute}}, t_{\text{memory}})\). Every step reads all the weights, which the whole batch shares, and every sequence's KV cache, which nobody shares. Weight reads stop dominating at a batch of about \(B^{*} \approx 300 \times N_{\text{total}}/N_{\text{active}}\) sequences. When HBM is full of KV cache, a step takes roughly 25 ms.

Part 1 treated the hardware as one big GPU with a total FLOPS and a total memory bandwidth. Real models are spread across many GPUs, and the way you cut a model up decides how much data has to move between them every step. This part looks at how mixture-of-experts (MoE) models are laid out, why one rack is the natural unit, and what you get when you spread a model across more than one rack.

  • The experts in an MoE layer are spread across GPUs, a few whole experts per GPU. Each token travels to whichever GPUs hold its experts and back. Any GPU may need to talk to any other, and a rack's NVLink switches provide exactly that. The network between racks is roughly ten times slower.
  • Layers can be split across racks, which is called pipeline parallelism. Each rack boundary carries one vector per token, against many vectors per token inside the rack, so the slow network keeps up easily.
  • In inference, pipelining doesn't change speed or cost. It only lowers the memory each rack needs for weights. The KV cache per GPU doesn't shrink at all.
  • So in practice you spread experts across a whole scale-up domain and pipeline as little as possible. The size of the scale-up domain sets the latency floor, because it decides how many GPUs read the weights in parallel.

What a mixture-of-experts layer does

In a dense transformer, every token goes through the same feed-forward block in every layer. In an MoE model, that block is replaced by many smaller blocks, the experts, and a small router that picks a few of them for each token.

Each expert is an ordinary MLP: an up projection, a nonlinearity, and a down projection. The router scores the experts for each token and keeps the top few. The chosen experts' outputs are added up, weighted by the router's scores, and the result is added back to the token through the residual connection. DeepSeek-V3 has 256 routed experts per layer and sends each token to 8 of them, plus one shared expert that every token goes through. The experts are also small. Each one has a hidden width of 2,048, against a model width of 7,168.

Spreading the experts across GPUs

The standard layout is expert parallelism: each GPU holds a few whole experts. Take DeepSeek-V3's 256 experts and a 72-GPU rack. 256 doesn't divide evenly by 72, so we use 64 GPUs and leave the other 8 idle or give them other work. That's 4 experts per GPU.

Every GPU also holds a slice of the batch and its own copy of the router, which is tiny. After routing, each token is sent to the GPUs that hold its experts, and the expert outputs are sent back. Which GPU sends to which depends on the router's decisions, so the traffic pattern is all-to-all. It's still much less traffic than sending every token everywhere. A DeepSeek-V3 token goes to 8 of 256 experts, so it visits at most 8 of the 64 GPUs.

What a rack is

All-to-all traffic wants every GPU connected directly to every other GPU, and that's what a rack-scale system like NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 is built for. Physically it's a cabinet a couple of meters tall that draws around 120 kW and weighs well over a tonne. It holds 18 compute trays with 4 GPUs each, and in the middle, 9 trays of NVLink switches. A spine of thousands of copper cables at the back connects every GPU to every switch, so any GPU can reach any other in two hops: up to a switch and back down. Each GPU gets 1.8 TB/s of NVLink bandwidth, 900 GB/s in each direction.

Leaving the rack is a different path. Each GPU also has a network card, at 400 or 800 Gb/s (50 to 100 GB/s), which goes up to switches shared with the rest of the data center. That's 9 to 18 times less bandwidth than NVLink. I'll call it 10 times. The fast in-rack network is called the scale-up network, and the slower one between racks is the scale-out network.

Why not wire thousands of GPUs to one giant switch? Mostly because of cables. Double the GPUs in a rack and you double the cables that have to run through the same backplane. Connector density, cable bend radius, weight, power delivery, and cooling are all pushed close to their limits in current racks. NVIDIA went from 8 GPUs per NVLink domain in Hopper servers to 72 in Blackwell largely by moving from a single server board to a whole-rack design, and its roadmap reaches larger domains with new, denser racks. Google's TPU pods connect thousands of chips with their fast interconnect, but as a 3D torus in which each chip links directly only to its neighbors, which suits all-to-all traffic less well than a switch.

Splitting an expert layer across two racks

Now suppose one expert layer is spread across two racks. On average, half of each token's expert visits land in the other rack, and with 8 experts per token almost every token needs at least one of them. That traffic has to cross the scale-out network at a tenth of the bandwidth, and the whole layer waits for it. So the scale-up domain is effectively the limit on how big an expert layer you can run comfortably. It's possible to go beyond it with enough engineering. DeepSeek, working with 8-GPU H800 servers, spread its decode experts across many servers over InfiniBand and wrote custom communication kernels to make that work. But you pay for it, and it's a big part of why larger scale-up domains have been worth so much.

Pipelining layers across racks

Experts are one way to cut a model. Layers are another. A model has dozens of layers, and nothing stops us from putting the first group on one rack, the next group on the next rack, and so on. That's pipeline parallelism. Does the slow network between racks become the bottleneck?

Count the vectors. Inside a rack, every MoE layer sends each token to its \(k\) experts and brings the results back, so that's \(2k\) vectors per token per layer over NVLink. With \(L\) layers per stage, it's \(2kL\) vectors per token per stage. At the rack boundary, each token crosses the network once, as a single vector. The network is about 10 times slower, so the time spent on the boundary is smaller than the time spent inside the rack when

\[ \frac{t_{\text{scale-up}}}{t_{\text{scale-out}}} \approx \frac{2kL}{\text{BW}_{\text{up}}/\text{BW}_{\text{out}}} \approx \frac{2kL}{10} \ \geq\ 1 \]

For DeepSeek-V3, \(k = 8\), so even one layer per stage gives \(16/10\). Any realistic number of layers per stage makes the rack boundary cheap. The layout that falls out mirrors the model itself: experts go on different GPUs, and layers go on different racks.

You could cut along other dimensions too. Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices across GPUs, along the model width or the expert's hidden width. That used to be common for dense models. With experts this small (a hidden width of 2,048), splitting them further costs more in communication than it saves.

What pipelining buys in inference

To keep all the racks busy, we split the batch into micro-batches and keep one micro-batch in each stage at a time. Decoding is a loop: when a micro-batch leaves the last stage with its new token, it goes straight back to the first stage to produce the next one.

As the figure shows, the number of micro-batches has to equal the number of stages. With fewer, a rack sits idle while it waits for the next micro-batch to come around.

What does this do to latency? A micro-batch passes through four racks, and each one runs a quarter of the layers, so the total time per token is the same as one rack running all the layers, plus a few network hops. Throughput is four times higher, but we're also using four times the hardware. In inference, pipelining neither speeds a token up nor makes it cheaper. What it saves is memory: each rack only holds a quarter of the weights.

What pipelining costs in training

Training is where pipelining gets painful. A training step runs the forward pass for the whole batch, then the backward pass, then updates the weights. The backward pass for a micro-batch can't start on a rack until the forward pass for it has finished on every later rack, and the weight update has to wait for every micro-batch's gradients.

The hatched region is the pipeline bubble. With \(P\) stages and \(M\) micro-batches in this simple schedule, the idle fraction is \((P-1)/(M+P-1)\), which is 3/7 in the figure. More micro-batches shrink the bubble, but you either grow the global batch or make each micro-batch smaller and less efficient. Smaller global batches are better for learning, since each update uses fresher gradients. The best choice balances these.

There are cleverer schedules, such as interleaved one-forward-one-backward, zero-bubble pipelines, and DeepSeek's DualPipe, which split the work more finely and overlap forward and backward passes to fill the gaps. They work, but they add a lot of complexity. They also constrain the architecture. A model with connections that skip across many layers is awkward to cut into stages. Pipelining is worth that trouble only when the model doesn't fit any other way.

Why pipelining doesn't shrink the KV cache

Back to inference. Pipelining saves memory on weights, so you might expect it to help with memory in general. Let's check. Spread the model over \(E\) GPUs per rack (the expert-parallel width) and \(P\) racks. The memory needed per GPU is the total divided by \(EP\):

\[ \text{memory per GPU} = \frac{\beta N_{\text{total}} + B\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}}{E\,P} \]

The problem is \(B\). We just saw that a pipeline needs one micro-batch per stage, and each micro-batch needs its own \(b \approx B^{*}\) sequences to amortize the weights in each stage. So the global batch is \(B = P\,b\). Substituting,

\[ \text{memory per GPU} = \frac{\beta N_{\text{total}}}{E\,P} + \frac{b\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}}{E} \]

The \(P\) cancels in the KV term.

The weight term keeps falling as you add stages. The KV term doesn't move. A natural objection: each stage only stores the KV cache for its own layers, so shouldn't the KV per rack shrink? It does, per sequence. But you now need \(P\) times as many sequences in flight to keep every stage busy, and the two effects cancel exactly. Just as no amount of batching shares a sequence's KV cache across the batch, no amount of pipelining spreads it more thinly per GPU.

For DeepSeek-V3 on 64 GPUs, the weights take about 10.5 GB per GPU out of 186 GB, so there's nothing to gain from pipelining at all. A model five times larger in total parameters would put about 52 GB of weights on each GPU, and splitting it over two racks would halve that. Pipelining is a fix for models whose weights don't fit comfortably. It does nothing for long contexts.

What gets used in practice

Put together, the layout for serving a large MoE model is simple. Use expert parallelism across the whole scale-up domain. Add pipeline stages only if the weights won't fit otherwise, and then only a couple. DeepSeek's published inference setup for V3, for example, uses wide expert parallelism for the MoE layers and no pipelining. Splitting individual experts with tensor parallelism has mostly faded, because the experts are already small.

Why bigger scale-up domains mattered

If pipelining solves capacity for weights, why was the jump from 8-GPU servers to 72-GPU racks such a big deal? Because of the latency floor from Part 1. The time to read all the weights once is

\[ t_{\text{floor}} = \frac{\beta N_{\text{total}}}{E \times \text{BW}_{\text{per GPU}}} \]

Only the GPUs in one stage read weights at the same time, because the stages run one after another. So the floor depends on the scale-up width \(E\), not on the total number of GPUs.

A trillion-parameter model in 8 bits on one 8-GPU H200 server fills almost all of its 1.1 TB of memory, leaving no room for KV cache, and it can't produce tokens for any one sequence faster than about 38 per second. On 64 GPUs of an NVL72, the same model's floor is about 2 ms, or 500 tokens per second. Pipelining across several H200 servers would fix the memory problem but not the speed problem.

This may be part of why frontier model sizes grew slowly for a while after GPT-4, which was widely reported to have well over a trillion parameters. A much larger sparse model would have been slow to serve on 8-GPU NVIDIA servers, and rack-scale NVLink only became mainstream with Blackwell. Google's TPU pods had large fast domains much earlier. Total parameter count is limited by what one scale-up domain can serve quickly. Active parameter count is limited by compute cost.

Next, in Part 3, we'll use this model to read API price sheets and work out what they reveal about KV cache sizes, prefill and decode, and where cached prompts are stored.

entry.title: What a Token Costs
entry.content:
Inference from First Principles 1. What a token costs 2. Fitting a model onto a rack 3. Reading the price sheet 4. Training a model you plan to serve

Part 1 of 4

A working model of LLM inference built from two hardware numbers and two model numbers, and what it says about batching, speed, and price.

Inference from First Principles · 6 diagrams

When Anthropic launched fast mode for Claude Opus 4.6, it charged six times the normal price per token for up to 2.5 times the output speed. Other coding tools sell similar tiers. That raises a few obvious questions. Why does paying more make tokens come out faster? Could you pay 100 times more and get tokens 100 times faster? And could you go the other way, accept a slow mode that takes minutes, and pay much less?

The answers come from a small model of how a transformer runs on a rack of GPUs. The same model explains why output tokens cost more than input tokens, why a cache hit costs a tenth of a normal input token or less, why very long contexts stay expensive, and why frontier models are trained on far more data than Chinchilla would suggest. This series builds that model from scratch.

This first part covers the core: two costs, two hardware limits, and the one knob that trades them off, which is batch size. Parts 2 to 4 apply it to hardware layout, API pricing, and training budgets.

The whole system on one page

Before any equations, here is the picture we're building toward.

Requests from many users arrive at a batcher. Every step, the batcher takes every sequence that's ready and runs them together through one forward pass of the model. That pass produces exactly one new token for each sequence, and then the next step starts. A step takes tens of milliseconds, so a sequence that's generating text goes around this loop about 40 times a second.

The model lives in a scale-up domain, which today usually means one rack of GPUs tied together by a fast switch. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 is the standard example: 72 GPUs, each with its own high-bandwidth memory (HBM). That HBM holds the model's weights, which every sequence shares, and the KV cache, which is a per-sequence record of every token the sequence has seen so far. Anything that has to leave the rack goes over a much slower network. KV caches that aren't in use can be parked in cheaper, slower memory such as host DRAM or flash.

Almost everything in this series comes from a handful of numbers about that picture.

Numbers to keep in your head

~300multiply-adds a GPU can do in the time it takes to read one weight from HBM
~25 mstime to read a GPU's entire HBM once, which sets the length of a decode step
~10×how much faster the network inside a rack is than the network between racks
18 to 32sparsity (total over active parameters) of DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2

One more model property shows up in Part 3: the size of the KV cache per token, which ranges from about 1 KB to over 300 KB depending on how attention is designed.

The rest of this post derives the following results.

  • Serving one sequence at a time costs hundreds to thousands of times more per token than serving a big batch, because every step has to read every weight no matter how many sequences share it.
  • There is a hard floor on latency: the time to read all the weights from HBM once. Fast modes buy speed by running smaller batches, which moves you toward that floor and spreads the fixed cost of a step over fewer tokens.
  • There is also a floor on cost. Once the batch is big enough, each token still needs its own multiply-adds and its own KV cache reads, and batching doesn't share those. A slow mode can't get much below that floor.
  • The batch size where weight reads stop dominating is about 300 times the model's sparsity. For DeepSeek-V3 that's around 5,000 sequences.
  • At scale, a decode step takes about as long as it takes to read all of HBM once, around 25 ms, because the memory fills up with KV cache and every step reads all of it.

Two costs and two hardware limits

Let's look at what one decode step does.

A sequence is a row of tokens. To produce the next token, the model takes the newest token and runs it through every layer, which means multiplying it by every weight matrix it's routed to. Inside each attention layer, the new token also looks back at every earlier token. It doesn't recompute those tokens. It reads the keys and values that were computed when each one was first processed, and that stored data is the KV cache. After the step, the new token's own keys and values are appended to it.

So each step does two kinds of work, and each is limited by a different part of the chip.

Compute

For every sequence in the batch, we multiply by all of the active parameters. A multiply-add counts as two floating-point operations, so for a batch of \(B\) sequences

\[ t_{\text{compute}} \approx \frac{2\,B\,N_{\text{active}}}{\text{FLOPS}} \]

Here \(N_{\text{active}}\) is the number of parameters a single token uses. In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that's much smaller than the total. DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters, but each token uses about 37 billion of them. FLOPS is the hardware's floating-point throughput, summed over all the GPUs holding one copy of the model.

I'm leaving out the multiply-adds inside attention itself. During decode, each byte of KV cache we read is used for only a handful of multiply-adds, so attention's cost shows up almost entirely as memory traffic, which we count next.

Memory

Every step has to stream all of the weights out of HBM, and for each sequence it has to stream that sequence's entire KV cache:

\[ t_{\text{memory}} \approx \frac{\beta\,N_{\text{total}} + B\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,s_{\text{kv}}}{\text{BW}} \]

The weight term uses \(N_{\text{total}}\), not \(N_{\text{active}}\). With a large batch, some token in the batch is routed to every expert, so every expert's weights get read. \(\beta\) is bytes per weight (1 for 8-bit weights, 0.5 for 4-bit). \(n_{\text{ctx}}\) is the context length in tokens, \(s_{\text{kv}}\) is the size of the KV cache per token in bytes, and BW is the total HBM bandwidth.

GPUs overlap memory transfers with math, so a step takes as long as the slower of the two:

\[ t_{\text{step}} \gtrsim \max\left(t_{\text{compute}},\ t_{\text{memory}}\right) \]

The \(\gtrsim\) is there because real systems never quite reach these limits. This is a roofline model. It ignores plenty, and it still predicts a surprising amount. In every term, the numerator describes the model and the denominator describes the hardware.

Batch size is the knob

Latency

Here is how each piece scales with batch size.

Compute time is a straight line through the origin: twice the batch, twice the multiply-adds. Memory time has a fixed part, the weights, which cost the same whether you serve one sequence or ten thousand, plus a KV part that grows with the batch. The step time is the upper envelope of the two.

Look at the left edge. Even with a batch of one, a step can't be faster than the time it takes to read every weight once. That's the latency floor for a given set of hardware. For a one-trillion-parameter model stored in 8 bits and spread across 64 Blackwell GPUs, each with 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth,

\[ \frac{10^{12}\ \text{bytes}}{64 \times 8\ \text{TB/s}} \approx 2\ \text{ms per step} \]

So no single sequence on that hardware gets more than about 500 tokens per second, whatever you pay. To go faster you need more total memory bandwidth (more GPUs reading weights in parallel, which Part 2 picks up), fewer bytes per weight, or a trick that produces more than one token per step, like speculative decoding.

Cost

Latency is what the user feels. Cost is what the provider pays, and it's easiest to see per token. Renting the hardware costs a fixed amount per second, and one step produces \(B\) tokens, so the cost per token is proportional to \(t_{\text{step}}/B\). Dividing every curve in Figure 3 by \(B\) gives this:

Compute per token is flat, since every token needs its own multiply-adds. KV reads per token are flat too, since each sequence reads its own cache. The weights are the only thing that gets shared, so their cost per token falls as \(1/B\). At small batches that hyperbola dominates and tokens are expensive. At large batches it fades away, and the cost settles onto a floor set by whatever each token can't share.

How much more expensive is a batch of one? At \(B=1\) each token pays for a full read of the weights. On the floor it pays only for its own multiply-adds. With short contexts, the ratio of the two works out to exactly the balance batch size \(B^{*}\) that we derive below, about 5,400 for DeepSeek-V3. With long contexts the floor also includes each token's KV reads, which shrinks the ratio. In the DeepSeek-V3 example later in this post it's about 300. Either way, serving one sequence at a time costs hundreds to thousands of times more per token.

Fast mode and slow mode

Now we can answer the opening questions. A fast mode moves left on these curves. The provider runs your requests in smaller batches, so each step reads less KV cache and finishes sooner. The weights still have to be read in full every step, and fewer tokens share that cost, so each token costs more.

How much more depends on how much of the step is weight reads. Take the DeepSeek-V3 example worked out later in this post, where a normal step takes 23.2 ms: 1.3 ms to read the weights and 21.9 ms to read KV cache. Write the step as a fixed weight-read time plus a KV-read time proportional to the batch, \(t = w + cB\). To make tokens 2.5 times faster, the step has to shrink to 9.3 ms. The weights still take 1.3 ms, so the KV reads have to drop to 8.0 ms, which takes a batch 2.7 times smaller. Cost per token is step time over batch size, so it changes by a factor of

\[ \frac{t_{\text{fast}}/B_{\text{fast}}}{t_{\text{normal}}/B_{\text{normal}}} = \frac{1}{2.5} \times 2.7 \approx 1.1 \]

That's only about 10% more per token. When KV reads dominate the step, a smaller batch removes KV reads and tokens in proportion, and only the weight reads get spread over fewer tokens. Fast mode gets expensive when the weights are a big share of the step, as with short contexts or very large models. Then each halving of the batch comes close to doubling the cost per token while buying little extra speed.

So the launch price, 6 times as much for 2.5 times the speed, isn't explained by the cost of a step alone. Some of it likely pays for capacity held in reserve, since batches only stay small if the provider doesn't fill them with other traffic, and some of it is margin on a new product. A provider can also put fast traffic on different hardware or lean harder on speculative decoding. Anthropic has since cut the premium, and fast mode on its newer Opus models costs about twice the normal price.

Why can't you pay 100 times more for 100 times the speed? Shrinking the batch only gets you down to the latency floor. In this example that's the 1.3 ms weight read, about 18 times faster than a normal step. Near the floor, batches are down to a handful of sequences, each token pays for nearly a whole weight read, and the cost per token climbs to hundreds of times normal. Past the floor you need more GPUs reading weights in parallel, fewer bytes per weight, or speculative decoding.

Slow mode is the reverse: bigger batches. That helps only until the weights are amortized. After that you're on the floor, paying for each token's own multiply-adds and its own KV reads, and waiting longer doesn't change either one. Batch APIs do sell a 50% discount for results within 24 hours, but that discount comes from scheduling. The provider fills hardware that would otherwise sit idle between traffic peaks. It doesn't come from making any single step cheaper.

Where the balance point is

The batch size that matters most is the one where weight reads stop dominating, the crossover \(B^{*}\) in the last two figures. Ignore the KV term for a moment and set the weight-read time equal to the compute time:

\[ \frac{\beta\,N_{\text{total}}}{\text{BW}} = \frac{2\,B\,N_{\text{active}}}{\text{FLOPS}} \]

Rearranging so the hardware is on one side and the model on the other,

\[ B^{*} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{FLOPS}/2}{\text{BW}/\beta}}_{\text{hardware}} \times \underbrace{\frac{N_{\text{total}}}{N_{\text{active}}}}_{\text{model}} \]

The hardware term is a plain number. The top is multiply-adds per second. The bottom is weights per second that HBM can deliver. Their ratio is how many multiply-adds the chip can do in the time it takes to load one weight. For an H100 running 8-bit math, that's 989 trillion multiply-adds per second against 3.35 trillion one-byte weights per second, about 295. For a Blackwell GPU in a GB200 NVL72 running 4-bit math, it's 5 quadrillion multiply-adds per second against 16 trillion half-byte weights per second (8 TB/s), about 310. Dropping to lower precision doubles the math and halves the bytes per weight, so the ratio barely moves. Call it 300.

The model term is the sparsity: how many parameters exist for every one a token uses. So

\[ B^{*} \approx 300 \times \frac{N_{\text{total}}}{N_{\text{active}}} \]
Model Total params Active params Sparsity \(B^{*}\)
Any dense model \(N\) \(N\) 1 ~300
DeepSeek-V3 671B 37B 18 ~5,400
Kimi K2 1.04T 32B 32 ~9,800

Model size isn't in that formula. A dense model of any size balances at a few hundred sequences, and it's sparsity that pushes the number into the thousands. In practice you'd run somewhat above \(B^{*}\), because real kernels don't reach the roofline, and the KV term we dropped also uses bandwidth, which pushes the crossover further right.

Keep in mind that \(B\) counts sequences, not tokens. A batch of 5,000 means 5,000 different conversations, each getting one more token in the same step.

If the context is long enough, the KV line in Figure 3 becomes steeper than the compute line, and then the step is memory-bound at every batch size. The DeepSeek-V3 example below is in that regime, and so is most long-context serving. Part 3 uses exactly this to read the size of a model's KV cache off its price list.

Why a step takes about 25 milliseconds

So far we've only used memory bandwidth. Memory capacity adds one more constraint, and it pins down the length of a step.

A provider wants big batches to amortize the weights, and it wants to support long contexts. Both mean more KV cache, so in practice the HBM fills up. Every step reads the entire KV cache of every sequence in the batch. If HBM is full and every step reads roughly all of it, the step time is capacity divided by bandwidth:

\[ t_{\text{step}} \approx \frac{\text{HBM capacity}}{\text{HBM bandwidth}} \]

That ratio has stayed in a narrow range. An H100 has 80 GB at 3.35 TB/s, which is 24 ms. A GB200 GPU has 186 GB at 8 TB/s, which is 23 ms. A B300 has 288 GB at 8 TB/s, which is 36 ms. So it's 20 to 40 milliseconds, and I'll use 25 ms as a round number. A step much longer than that would need more data than the memory can hold.

Let's check this against a real model. Put DeepSeek-V3 in 8-bit on 64 GB200 GPUs (its 256 experts divide evenly into 64, as Part 2 explains). Total HBM is 11.9 TB. The weights take 0.67 TB, and the other 11.2 TB holds KV cache. At \(B \approx 5{,}400\), that's about 2 GB of cache per sequence, or about 30,000 tokens of context at DeepSeek-V3's roughly 70 KB per token.

Weight reads and multiply-adds are balanced, as designed, at about 1.3 ms each. The KV reads take 22 ms. At scale, decode spends almost all of its time reading KV cache. That fact sits behind a lot of the pricing in Part 3, starting with why output tokens cost more than input tokens.

Batches leave on a timetable

If a step takes 25 ms, what happens to a request that arrives in the middle of one? Think of each step as a train. A train leaves every 25 ms whether or not it's full. Any sequence that's ready gets on, and if the train is full, it waits for the next one.

The worst case is a request that arrives just after a train leaves. It waits up to one step for the next departure and then one more step for its token, about 50 ms in total. That's small next to network latency and the time it takes to process a long prompt. Batching costs users very little in waiting time. What they notice is mostly the step time itself.

The timetable also gives the throughput of one copy of the model: \(B\) tokens every step. At \(B \approx 5{,}400\) and 25 ms, that's about 216,000 tokens per second. Google said in May 2026 that it was processing more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, which is about 1.2 billion per second. That count includes input tokens, so it isn't a like-for-like comparison, but one efficient replica is clearly a tiny slice of a large provider. For a small provider it sets a minimum. Without about 200,000 tokens per second of steady demand per replica, you can't fill the batch, and every token costs more.

Where the series goes from here

The next three parts apply this model.

  • Part 2 looks at how a model is laid out on GPUs, why a single rack is the natural unit for MoE models, and why pipelining across racks helps with weights but not with KV cache.
  • Part 3 reads API price sheets with this model and recovers the KV cache size per token and the kind of storage behind prompt caching.
  • Part 4 works out how much to train a model that will be served at this scale, and finds that frontier models are probably trained on hundreds of times more data than Chinchilla-optimal.

Diagrams are drawn in TikZ.

entry.title: DeepSeek’s Super-agent, explained
entry.content:
DeepSeek’s Harness team has designed a single coding agent that lives in a team’s chat and GitHub repository and handles many requests in parallel.

Based on the team’s design essay and open-source prototype, both published October 31, 2026, and on press coverage from November 1.

Overview

DeepSeek Harness (the dsh command) is DeepSeek’s open-source agent harness, the program around a model that reads your request, calls tools, runs commands, saves the session and repeats until the job is done. It came out in August 2026 under the MIT licence. Every part of it, from the model adapter to the agent loop, is a plugin you can replace.

Super-agent is what the Harness team wants to build next. Today you open one chat session per task. In their design, one agent sits in the team’s group chat and GitHub repository, picks up requests, starts workers for them in parallel, and replies in the thread where it was asked.

The team shipped two things: a long design essay and a prototype, dsh-superagent-prototype, packaged as a Harness bundle for one GitHub repository with optional Feishu chat. Both are labelled as research, and the prototype covers only part of what the essay describes.

The essay’s rule is to spend as little human attention as possible for as much value as possible. The agent acts only when asked or when a written team rule allows it, and posts only when someone has to act or can use the result.

Attention is the bottleneck

Today’s coding agents treat one session as one unit of work. Sessions don’t share memory, so when you run several in parallel you are the one carrying context between them and switching back and forth. The team puts the limit at about three to five sessions that one person can actively follow. Past that, more agents don’t get more done, because you can’t keep up with them.

The essay asks for an agent with one memory across conversations and channels, that runs many tasks at once, notices work nobody assigned, and stays online. Its example is a group that agrees on plan A in chat and then switches to plan B in a pull-request comment. The agent should see that both are about the same work and change course.

Architecture

The essay compares two simple designs before settling on a third.

The Router is one long-lived session. It receives every human message from every channel, keeps track of how tasks relate, decides who does what, and is the only part that talks to people. It doesn’t write code and may not have a shell tool at all. The team found the job easier than they expected, and a smaller, faster model often handles it well.

Each Worker gets a fresh context, the full tool set, and usually the strongest model, since Workers write the code. They never message people. They report to the Router, which answers for them. Inside a hard task a Worker can still start its own sub-agents or an agent team, and the Router never sees that detail.

In a typical “agent team”, a lead agent breaks one big task into parts and coordinates them closely. The Router never splits a task. It tracks how separate tasks relate to each other.

Choosing what to work on

Every piece of work starts as a trigger, such as a chat message, an email, a calendar reminder, a code-review comment or a CI result. Most of what happens in a group chat isn’t a request, so triggers pass two filters. The fast path is ordinary code that lets events through by source, group and allow-list. Whatever gets past it goes to the slow path, where an LLM reads the team’s written policy and decides whether to take the work on.

The prototype spells out who can start work. An explicit request is a person on the allow-list addressing the agent, and it is handled in every mode. An inferred candidate is something the agent noticed on its own, and it needs a matching written rule. Messages from bots always count as inferred candidates.

Inferred work then depends on the accept mode. off ignores it. observe, the default, records “would have accepted” and runs nothing. auto actually starts the work. The README suggests running in observe first, reading what it would have done, and switching to auto after that. Each work item also records which version of the policy it was accepted under, so tightening a rule can revoke work before it resumes.

Threads

Consecutive events in the same pull request, chat topic or email chain form a thread. The first event goes through the Router, which starts a Worker and subscribes it to that thread. Later events in that thread go straight to the Worker without passing through the Router.

Subscriptions are many-to-many. Two Workers subscribed to the same thread both see its events, so they find out they are touching the same code without messaging each other. In the experiments, turning direct delivery off barely changed how fast tasks finished, but the Router had to make about 30% more decisions and read about 37% more tokens.

Memory

A Router that runs for weeks can’t keep everything in its context. The team treats the context window as a cache. Some information is placed in it directly, the rest is left out behind a reference, and every object has an ID the model can use to look it up.

When someone asks in chat whether “the font thing” is done, the Router doesn’t need last week’s conversation in memory. The message carries a thread ID, the thread carries the Worker’s ID, and the Worker’s record points at the pull request, where the answer is.

An asynchronous agent loop

Most agents run a ReAct loop: think, call a tool, wait for the result, think again. While a long build runs, the agent can’t read new messages. Super-agent replaces long commands and subtasks with start() and stop(). start() returns “Started” immediately, the result comes back later as a new event, and the model can cancel something that’s taking too long or is no longer wanted.

This asynchronous mode already exists in DeepSeek Harness but is off by default. The Router uses the same mechanism to batch work. Triggers that arrive while it is in the middle of a call are added to its next one.

Where it runs

To keep the agent online, the design separates compute from storage, as many databases do. The code that drives the agent loop runs in stateless cloud containers. Every session’s state lives in a database. If a container crashes, another one loads the state and continues.

The machines that do the work only run a small daemon that executes commands and returns results. That means your own laptop, with its uncommitted changes and local credentials, can be one of the machines the agent runs commands on. If a device goes offline, its tasks wait and catch up when it reconnects. The essay compares this to Anthropic’s “brain and hands” split, with the difference that the hands here are people’s own computers instead of hosted sandboxes.

The Watchdog

A separate Watchdog session runs on a timer. It handles infrastructure failures like API errors or failed state recovery, and it checks whether each Worker is making real progress or drifting. Maintainers can ask it in plain language why something failed and have it adjust prompts or trigger rules.

An example request

Here is how a bug report moves through the system. A person is involved in only a few of the steps.

The agent writes differently in each channel. Chat replies are informal and stay under 100 words. On GitHub and email it writes longer, structured text, for example a pull-request description with background, changes and how the fix was tested.

DeepSeek also uses the agent for speculative work. Their Harness user group has a “silently reproduce and fix” rule: when someone reports a problem, the agent tries to reproduce and fix it in the background and says nothing unless it confirms the bug and finds a simple fix. In one case, people were still discussing a bug where tildes rendered as strikethrough when the agent opened a pull request fixing it.

Results

The team ran a synthetic test. Each run fed in about 300 chat and CI messages, of which about 20 were real work requests and the rest chatter, follow-ups, stop requests and CI noise. The coding itself was replaced by a tool that waits for a set time, so the test measures scheduling and coordination and says nothing about code quality. Each setup ran five times.

With a neutral prompt, the model never used its sub-agent tool in five runs, so everything happened in one session that kept getting interrupted. With a “delegate first” prompt it delegated in four of five runs. In the fifth it decided a task was small enough to do itself, and that run was the slowest.

A separate stress test looked only at the Router. As triggers rose from about 1 to about 40 per minute, it grouped more of them into each model call (from 1.0 to 2.8 on average). Time per request rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds, while time per decision fell from 6.4 to 1.6 seconds. The team concluded that one Router session is enough for a team their size.

The authors call these results preliminary, given the synthetic load and simplified environment.

Sources

  • AgentsPulse: review of the design essay, with the experiment numbers
  • Developers Digest: what the prototype ships, its accept modes and execution caveats
  • deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype on GitHub
  • The original design essay (Chinese, WeChat)
  • i-SCOOP: the attention-budget framing
  • Bloomberg: news coverage of the release
  • DeepSeek Harness

Written from public sources as of November 1, 2026. All numbers come from the DeepSeek Harness team.

Claude Code is a terminal-based AI coding assistant built as a TypeScript application with a custom React/Ink TUI (Terminal User Interface). The architecture follows a layered pattern:

  2. Bootstrap loads configuration, telemetry, auth, and networking
  3. Setup prepares the working directory, hooks, plugins, and file watchers
  4. UI Layer renders the terminal interface using a custom Ink/React renderer
  5. QueryEngine orchestrates the conversation: sending messages to Claude, streaming responses, and executing tools
  6. Tool System provides 50+ tools the model can invoke, each with its own permission logic
  7. Services & State underpin everything: API clients, analytics, MCP servers, memory, history

Narrative

The query loop is an async generator — it yields streaming events as they arrive from the Claude API, allowing the UI to render responses incrementally. When Claude’s response includes tool_use blocks (e.g., “read this file” or “run this command”), the loop pauses streaming, executes the tools (with permission checks), and then loops back to send the tool results to Claude. This continues until Claude responds with just text (no tool calls), at which point the loop terminates.

The loop also handles recovery: if the context gets too long, it compacts the conversation history. If the model hits output limits, it escalates. If the user interrupts, it aborts gracefully.

9. Narrative Walkthrough: A Message End-to-End

Let’s trace exactly what happens when you type "Fix the bug in auth.ts" and press Enter.

Step 1: Input Capture (Presentation Layer)

Your keystrokes flow through Ink’s custom event system → PromptInput component → TextInput with history support. When you press Enter, handlePromptSubmit() in utils/handlePromptSubmit.ts is called. It checks for slash commands (none here), and passes the raw text to the REPL’s message handler.

Step 2: Message Creation (Application Layer)

The REPL creates a UserMessage with your text as a TextBlock. It adds the message to the conversation history and records it to the session transcript (async, fire-and-forget for performance).

Step 3: Context Gathering (Application Layer)

Before calling the API, the system gathers context:

  • System context: git status (branch, recent commits, dirty files)
  • User context: contents of CLAUDE.md files found in the project, current date
  • System prompt: the full system prompt including tool descriptions, permission rules, and behavioral instructions

This context is memoized per session — computed once, then cached.

Step 4: API Call (Infrastructure Layer)

QueryEngine.submitMessage() delegates to query() which calls queryLoop(). The loop calls deps.callModel() which maps to queryModelWithStreaming in services/api/claude.ts. This makes a streaming POST to the Anthropic Messages API with:

  • The full conversation history (normalized)
  • The system prompt
  • All 50+ tool schemas
  • Model selection and thinking configuration

Step 5: Streaming Response (Application → Presentation)

As tokens arrive from the API, the async generator yields them. Each yield updates the UI in real-time — you see Claude’s response character by character. The Messages.tsx component renders each AssistantMessage with Markdown.tsx for formatting and HighlightedCode.tsx for code blocks.

Step 6: Tool Calls (Application → Domain → Infrastructure)

Claude decides it needs to read the file first. Its response includes:

{ "type": "tool_use", "name": "Read", "input": { "file_path": "/project/auth.ts" } }

The query loop detects this and enters tool execution:

  1. toolOrchestration.ts finds FileReadTool by name
  2. FileReadTool.validateInput() checks the path is valid
  3. FileReadTool.checkPermissions() — reading is typically allowed
  4. Pre-tool hooks fire (if configured in settings)
  5. FileReadTool.call() reads the file from disk
  6. Post-tool hooks fire
  7. The file contents are returned as a tool_result message

Step 7: Loop Back (Application Layer)

The tool result is added to the message history. The query loop sends the entire updated history (including the tool result) back to the Claude API. Claude now has the file contents and can analyze the bug.

Claude might then call FileEdit to fix the bug, triggering another round of tool execution. This time, the permission system shows a dialog because file editing requires user approval (in default mode). You see the proposed diff and press ‘y’ to approve.

Step 8: Completion (Application → Presentation)

After fixing the file, Claude responds with just text (no more tool calls): “I’ve fixed the authentication bug in auth.ts. The issue was…“. The query loop detects no tool_use blocks and returns Terminal { reason: 'completed' }. The UI shows Claude’s final message and re-displays the input prompt.

Step 9: Persistence (Infrastructure Layer)

Throughout this flow, several things were persisted:

  • Transcript: Full conversation saved to ~/.claude/projects/{hash}/ as JSONL
  • History: Your input “Fix the bug in auth.ts” added to ~/.claude/history.jsonl
  • Analytics: Events logged (session, tool use, model, tokens, cost)
  • File state: The read file cached in FileStateCache (LRU) for subsequent reads
  • Cost: Token usage tracked in cost-tracker.ts and displayed in StatusLine

Why Is It Structured This Way?

  1. Async generators everywhere: The streaming nature of LLM responses demands non-blocking, incremental processing. Async generators let the query loop yield events to the UI as they arrive, rather than waiting for the full response.

  2. Custom Ink renderer: Terminal UIs need pixel-level control. The custom Ink implementation (based on React reconciliation + Yoga layout) gives Claude Code the same component model as web React, but targeting terminal cells instead of DOM nodes.

  3. Tool interface as the core abstraction: By making every capability a Tool with a uniform interface (schema, permissions, execution), the system can add new tools without changing the query loop, permission system, or UI rendering. MCP tools from external servers plug in identically.

  4. Multi-layer permission system: Security is critical for a code agent. The cascading permission model (rules → tool logic → mode → classifier → user) balances safety with usability — safe operations auto-approve, dangerous ones require explicit consent.

  5. Feature flags via compile-time elimination: Bun’s feature() intrinsic lets Anthropic ship a single binary with 108+ internal modules completely stripped out. The published CLI contains zero internal code — it’s all dead-code-eliminated at build time.

  6. Bootstrap state as global mutable singleton: While controversial, this pattern enables fast startup (no DI container) and easy access from any module. The bootstrap/state.ts file is the “session object” that everything reads from.

  7. Fire-and-forget parallelism: Startup parallelizes aggressively — network pre-connection, auth prefetch, repository detection, and command loading all run concurrently. This is why Claude Code starts fast despite doing a lot of initialization.

Input Schema

Defined via Zod with the following parameters:

Parameter Purpose
pattern Regex pattern (ripgrep syntax, not POSIX grep)
path Directory or file to search (defaults to CWD)
glob File filter like "*.ts" or "*.{js,tsx}"
type Ripgrep file type shorthand (js, py, rust)
output_mode files_with_matches (default), content, or count
-A/-B/-C/context Context lines around matches (content mode only)
-n Line numbers (defaults true, content mode only)
-i Case-insensitive search
multiline Enable cross-line matching (-U --multiline-dotall)
head_limit Cap results (default 250, 0 = unlimited)
offset Skip first N entries (for pagination)

The schema uses semanticNumber and semanticBoolean wrappers that handle the model sending strings like "true" or "3" instead of actual booleans/numbers.

Execution Flow

  GrepTool.call()
       │
       ├── 1. BUILD RIPGREP ARGS
       │   ├── Always: --hidden, --max-columns 500
       │   ├── Auto-exclude VCS dirs: .git, .svn, .hg, .bzr, .jj, .sl
       │   ├── Map output_mode → rg flags (-l, -c, or default)
       │   ├── If pattern starts with "-" → use -e flag
       │   ├── Apply glob filters (split on spaces, preserve brace patterns)
       │   ├── Apply permission-based ignore patterns (e.g. node_modules, .env)
       │   └── Exclude orphaned plugin cache directories
       │
       ├── 2. SPAWN RIPGREP (ripgrep.ts)
       │   ├── Resolve rg binary (system → embedded → builtin vendor)
       │   ├── Timeout: 20s (60s on WSL), configurable via env var
       │   ├── Buffer: 20MB max stdout
       │   ├── On EAGAIN error → retry with -j 1 (single-threaded)
       │   ├── On timeout with no output → throw RipgrepTimeoutError
       │   └── On macOS → auto-codesign vendored binary if needed
       │
       └── 3. PROCESS RESULTS (by output_mode)
           │
           ├── files_with_matches (default):
           │   ├── stat() each file (Promise.allSettled, tolerates deletions)
           │   ├── Sort by modification time (most recent first)
           │   ├── Apply head_limit/offset pagination
           │   └── Convert to relative paths
           │
           ├── content:
           │   ├── Apply head_limit/offset first (avoid wasted path conversion)
           │   └── Convert absolute paths in "path:line:content" to relative
           │
           └── count:
               ├── Apply head_limit/offset
               ├── Convert paths to relative
               └── Parse "path:count" lines → total matches + file count

Ripgrep Binary Resolution (src/utils/ripgrep.ts)

The getRipgrepConfig() function (memoized, resolved once per process) picks the rg binary in priority order:

  1. System — user’s installed rg (used if USE_BUILTIN_RIPGREP is not set to falsy). Uses just the command name rg rather than the resolved path to prevent PATH hijacking.
  2. Embedded — in the production Bun build, ripgrep is statically compiled into the binary. Spawned via argv0='rg' so the Bun process dispatches to the embedded rg.
  3. Builtin — vendored platform-specific binary from vendor/ripgrep/{arch}-{platform}/rg.

Error Recovery

The ripgrep wrapper has several resilience mechanisms:

  • EAGAIN retry: Resource-constrained environments (Docker, CI) can fail with “resource temporarily unavailable” when rg spawns too many threads. The wrapper detects this and retries with -j 1 (single-threaded) for that call only — it doesn’t persist single-threaded mode globally, which would cause timeouts on large repos.
  • Timeout with partial results: If rg times out but has partial stdout, the last line is dropped (may be incomplete) and the partial results are returned. If there’s no output at all, a RipgrepTimeoutError is thrown so the model knows the search didn’t complete (vs. thinking there were no matches).
  • Buffer overflow: At 20MB stdout, partial results are returned with the last line dropped.
  • File deletion races: files_with_matches mode uses Promise.allSettled for stat calls, so a file deleted between rg’s scan and the stat doesn’t crash the whole search — it just gets mtime: 0.

Pagination System

The default head_limit of 250 prevents context bloat — unbounded content-mode greps can fill the 20KB tool-result persistence threshold (6–24K tokens). When truncation occurs, appliedLimit is set in the output:

[Showing results with pagination = limit: 250]

This tells the model “there are more results.” It can then call Grep again with offset: 250 to see the next page. This is how the model implements multi-round search — paginating through large result sets across multiple tool calls.

Result Formatting

mapToolResultToToolResultBlockParam() formats output into text tool_result blocks sent back to Claude:

  • files_with_matches: "Found 5 files\nsrc/a.ts\nsrc/b.ts\n..." — files sorted by mtime (most recently modified first, a heuristic that the most task-relevant files were touched recently)
  • content: Matching lines with relative paths and line numbers
  • count: "src/a.ts:12\nsrc/b.ts:3\n\nFound 15 total occurrences across 2 files."

If results exceed maxResultSizeChars (20,000 chars), the tool system persists them to disk and sends Claude a preview + filepath instead, preventing context window overflow.

Permission & Security

  • validateInput() checks the path exists, suggests corrections if not found, and blocks UNC paths (\\server\share) to prevent NTLM credential leaks on Windows
  • checkPermissions() delegates to checkReadPermissionForTool() — standard read-permission check against toolPermissionContext
  • preparePermissionMatcher() enables wildcard permission rules like Grep(*.env) to deny searching sensitive file patterns
  • Permission-based ignore patterns from settings (e.g., node_modules, .env files) are automatically applied as --glob !pattern arguments
  • The tool’s prompt explicitly instructs the model to never run grep or rg via BashTool — always use this tool, which enforces the correct permission and ignore-pattern rules

Tool Properties

  isConcurrencySafe: true    ← multiple Greps run in parallel batches
  isReadOnly: true           ← no filesystem mutations
  maxResultSizeChars: 20,000 ← results >20K persisted to disk
  strict: true               ← no extra input fields allowed

11. Deep Dive: Memory Management & Context Compaction

Claude Code operates within a finite context window (e.g., ~200K tokens). Conversations with heavy tool use can fill this quickly. The system uses a multi-layered compaction strategy that operates at three timescales to keep conversations going indefinitely.

The Problem

Without compaction, long sessions would hit the context limit and stop working. The system must compress old context while preserving the information the model needs to continue working effectively.
